bibliographic_review_management.status_rationale: Retained as supporting: it directly addresses nanosatellite electrical architecture/EPS modeling, power-budget generation, toolchain interoperability, and pre-physical simulation, but provides limited formal MBSE method and validation evidence.
bibliographic_review_management.citation: Boan, P. (2025). Concurrent Engineering Process for Electrical Architecture of Nanosatellites Preliminary Phases. DOI: 10.1117/12.3062667.
bibliographic_review_management.title: CONCURRENT ENGINEERING PROCESS FOR ELECTRICAL ARCHITECTURE OF NANOSATELLITES PRELIMINARY PHASES

RQ1.rationale: The paper shows how to model a nanosatellite mission and EPS/electrical architecture using a common technical reference, mode-based power budgets, ephemeris-derived flows, and Opalis simulations, but does not explicitly frame the method as a general minimal-behavior-knowledge reference model.

RQ2.rationale: It claims integrability, smooth workflow, rapid change analysis, and sizing/trade-off value from model-enabled tools; reliability is only indirectly addressed through SOC/energy margins and reproducibility is weakly supported by file-standard discussion.

RQ3.rationale: Pre-physical verification is represented by energy-balance and worst-case battery simulations with SOC thresholds, but the paper does not provide a formal verification model, requirements trace, or physical test integration.

bibliographic_review_management.lineage_overlap_notes: No other papers or previous extractions were consulted. Possible overlap with other CNES concurrent-engineering or Opalis work is not assessed under the silo rule.

RQ1: A nanosatellite mission can be represented as a common technical reference combining system/subsystem description, geometry, mission scenario, ephemeris, attitude, and system budgets.

The EPS/electrical architecture is modeled at preliminary level with a power-subsystem model, mode-based power profile, and ephemeris-derived energy flows rather than detailed behavioral models for every subsystem.
Generality is pursued through standardized files, plugins, and common database handoffs, but the paper does not define a reusable formal reference model.
RQ2: Claimed value centers on integrability/interoperability, adaptability, rapid change analysis, parallel trade-offs, and preliminary sizing.
Reliability-related value is indirect: SOC/DoD margins and survival/no-illumination simulation indicate energy margin, but no reliability metric or operational evidence is reported.
Reproducibility is limited: standard files and tool roles are described, but model files and complete schemas are not provided.
RQ3: Verification before physical development is implemented through Opalis energy-balance simulations driven by model-generated power profiles and energy-flow inputs.
Worst-case illumination and survival scenarios use SOC thresholds to assess feasibility and battery margin.
The paper does not report formal requirements verification, hardware-in-the-loop, integration tests, or flight validation.

author_stated_limitations_gaps: The described process is for preliminary phases.
The use case is a single 16U nanosatellite mission concept evaluated for feasibility by CNES with LESIA.
The power-subsystem sizing scenario is reduced to a 48-hour worst-case illumination period considered representative of the whole mission.
Extension to phases A/B/C/D is conditional on adding a satellite manufacturer/provider and preserving the file standard.
extractor_identified_limitations_gaps: Venue and publisher are not reported in the paper markdown or supplied citation metadata.
No formal MBSE language, metamodel, requirements repository, or traceability matrix is reported.
No executable model files, data schemas, repositories, or open datasets are provided.

Simulation conclusions depend on tool models and assumptions that are not independently validated in the paper.

direct_evidence_quotes.quote: The objective of this paper is to describe the approach through the prism of an electrical architect, that contributes to needs analysis, realization of power budgets, system sizing and energetic simulations through a specific use case.

The selected use case to illustrate this paper is a 16U nanosatellite operating on low-earth orbit its mission being the 3D mapping of hot stars dynamic environment by using ultraviolet spectropolarimetry measurements from space for the first time.

The overall concurrent engineering approach consists in setting up a common technical reference (satellite description and mission), with the aim of producing system-level budgets (mass, power, centering/inertias, data, etc.) produced by the various subsystems experts/architects.
The model is defined in the Opalis software. It is a proprietary but open tool developed by CNES that allows performing power simulations.
The main added value of this process is that it allows to define an adaptable and interoperable model.

Flight dynamics experts from CNES thus extracted from the global observation plan provided by the LESIA the worst case scenarios in terms of sun illumination, reducing it to a period of 48h only that could be used to size the power subsystem and still be representative of the whole mission.

The ultimate goal of the simulation process is to refine the power subsystem definition and to size elements (in particular cells and accumulators assemblies for solar panels and battery) in order to reach an energy balance between generation, storage and usage.
